overview: The Arikara, who also call themselves Sahnish, built farming villages along the Missouri River and sustained trade across the Plains. The imported outline shows one portion of their changing river homeland, not every place they lived. They are a distinct people within today’s Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation; the map dates do not mark their origin or disappearance.

periods.summary: Gardens, bison hunts and trade supported communities whose locations changed over time.

periods.title: Trade, war and epidemic disease
periods.summary: Conflict with traders and devastating epidemics brought further movements and rebuilding.

periods.title: Alliance and reservation life
periods.summary: Arikara communities joined their Mandan and Hidatsa neighbors and adapted to reservation farming.

periods.summary: The Garrison project displaced communities; families rebuilt while continuing their languages and government.

sections.title: A river home and a working household

items.text: The Sahnish migration tradition gives their journey a purpose: guidance from Chief Above and Mother Corn. MHA Nation’s history presents this as a community account of how the people came to their homeland. It places movement within responsibility and sacred relationships, rather than describing people as wandering without direction.

Arikara women planted gardens in the river bottomlands. Families left for summer bison hunts and returned for harvest, with another hunt before winter. A year’s food therefore depended on both cultivated plants and carefully timed travel. Cornfields and hunting camps belonged to the same working calendar.

Inside an earthlodge, beds stood along the outer wall while people cooked and sat near the central fire. A roof opening let smoke escape and light enter. Women built these homes from wood and earth, arranging space for ordinary family life as well as sacred objects.

Women made decorated clay cooking pots and willow harvest baskets. The baskets’ brown and white geometric patterns were woven around wooden frames. Houses could shelter several generations, often sisters and their families, so cooking, storage and childcare were part of a busy shared household.

Fresh meat did not have to be eaten all at once. Arikara women cut bison meat into thin strips and hung it on racks to dry; a small fire could help. The dried meat could later go into stew. Preparing tomorrow’s food began well before tomorrow.

Surplus crops helped make Arikara villages important trading places. The Kansas Historical Society describes exchanges with peoples including the Kiowa and Cheyenne when relations were peaceful. Food grown beside the Missouri could support wider networks linking gardeners, hunters and traveling traders.

As reservation agriculture changed, Arikara men increasingly farmed and ranched, while many women continued family gardens. North Dakota’s historical teaching collection explicitly records that persistence around 1900. A new farm economy did not instantly replace the household knowledge that had fed people for generations.

sections.title: Village memories, upheaval and living language

items.text: A village map became much more informative when a former resident explained it. In 1908, Bull Neck spoke with A. B. Stout through interpreter Alex Sage about Star Village, an Arikara settlement of the early 1860s. Their work identified occupants of 22 of its 94 lodges.

Those notes distinguish people’s homes from other village buildings. The rectangular structure numbered 26 was Sun’s horse stable, while White Eagle’s lodge served as a council place. Family testimony lets an archaeological plan recover something of how neighbors actually used the settlement.

The Arikara War of 1823 involved trade as well as fighting. Arikara people defended their position in Missouri commerce as American trappers tried to reach trading partners beyond them. An attack on William Ashley’s party brought a punitive expedition combining United States troops, traders and Lakota allies.

The campaign did not end with a simple surrender. The Arikara left their villages, and after the troops withdrew, trader Joshua Pilcher burned the settlements on August 15, 1823. Leaving one devastated village was part of a longer history of survival and rebuilding along the river.

Smallpox swept through the Missouri communities in 1837. The following year, Arikara people moved into the largely abandoned Mandan village near Fort Clark. Disease and conflict prompted further moves; in the early 1860s they settled beside Mandan and Hidatsa neighbors at Like-a-Fishhook Village.

Garrison Dam transformed the Missouri valley again in the 1950s. In 2007 testimony, tribal chairman Marcus Wells Jr. described the loss of fertile bottomlands and the relocation of 339 families across the three affiliated tribes. Floodwater separated communities and made journeys to services longer; this figure includes all three nations.

An Arikara expression printed by MHA Nation is “wetAxkoosšteéRAt!”, translated “Thank you!” The unusual-looking mix of capital and lowercase letters is retained from the community’s language page. This is a modern teaching witness, not an invented reconstruction of a sentence from the map’s earliest year.

The same language program makes recorded Arikara lessons and learning materials available for people who cannot attend a class. Its resources sit alongside separate Mandan and Hidatsa language work. The shared government supports three distinct linguistic inheritances, giving learners more ways to hear and practice their own.

ending.text: Arikara people did not disappear in 1783. War, epidemics, reservation policies and reservoir flooding changed where and how families lived. Sahnish identity and language continue within the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation, with community teaching carrying knowledge to new generations.
